hello.title: Hello, TypeScript
hello.summary: Print your first lines, store values with let and const, and add your first type annotations.
hello.lesson.0: TypeScript is JavaScript with **types**. Before your program runs, a tool called the **type checker** reads your code and warns you about mistakes. Then the types are removed and the code runs as normal JavaScript.
hello.lesson.2: `console.log` prints a value and then starts a new line. You can print several values at once: separate them with commas, and they appear with a space between them. Text goes in quotes, numbers do not, so `2 + 3` is calculated.
hello.lesson.4: A **variable** stores a value under a name. `const` creates a variable that you cannot reassign. `let` creates a variable that you can change later. Use `const` by default and `let` only when the value must change.
hello.lesson.6: Strings written between backticks are **template strings**. Inside them, `${...}` inserts the value of a variable or expression into the text.
hello.lesson.9: After a variable name you can write a colon and a type, for example `let age: number = 36;`. This is a **type annotation**. The three basic types are `number` for numbers, `string` for text and `boolean` for `true` or `false`.
hello.lesson.11: The type checker uses annotations to find mistakes. Here `count` is a `number`, so putting the string `"five"` into it is an error. The type checker reports it before the program ever runs.
hello.lesson.13: Type annotations exist only for the type checker. When the code runs, they are removed. They never change what your program prints.
hello.card.2: `let age: number = 36;` is a type annotation
hello-1.explain: `4 * 3` is calculated first, then `console.log` prints both values with a space between them.
hello-2.prompt: Which keyword creates a variable that you cannot reassign?
hello-2.explain: `const` creates a variable that keeps its value. Use `let` when the value must change.
hello-3.statement: Type annotations change what the program prints.
hello-3.explain: Annotations are only read by the type checker. They are removed before the code runs.
hello-4.prompt: Complete the annotation so that `price` holds a number.
hello-4.explain: `9.5` is a number, so the type is `number`. The other types do not accept a number.
hello-5.prompt: Which line does the type checker reject?
hello-5.explain: `total` is a `number`, but `"10"` is a string. Write `total = 10;` without quotes.
hello-6.prompt: Build a line that creates a constant `city` of type `string` with the value `"Oslo"`.
hello-6.explain: `const` makes a constant, `: string` is the annotation and `=` gives the value.
hello-7.prompt: Put the lines in order so that the program prints `Score: 30`.
hello-7.explain: First create `score`, then add 5 to get 15, then double it to get 30, and print it at the end.
hello-8.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
hello-9.explain: Each `${...}` inserts a value. `${n + n}` calculates `8` before it is inserted.
hello-10.options.2: The type checker reports an error
hello-10.explain: `max` is a `const`, so it cannot get a new value. Use `let` if the value must change.
hello-11.explain: Without quotes, `2 + 3` is a calculation, so it prints `5`. To print the text, write `"2 + 3"`.
types.title: Basic types
types.summary: Use number, string and boolean, typed arrays and tuples, let TypeScript infer types, and compare any with unknown.
types.lesson.0: Every value has a type. The `typeof` operator tells you the type of a value while the program runs. It gives the name of the type as a string.
types.lesson.2: Comparisons give a `boolean`. Use `>`, `<`, `>=` and `<=` to compare numbers, `===` to test if two values are equal and `!==` to test if they are different. The `+` operator also joins strings.
types.lesson.4: If you give a variable a value right away, TypeScript works out its type for you. This is called **type inference**. Here `count` gets the type `number` without an annotation, so `count = "six"` would be an error.
types.lesson.7: An **array** is a list of values. Its type is the type of the elements followed by `[]`, for example `number[]` or `string[]`. Positions start at `0`, `length` is the number of elements and `push` adds an element at the end.
types.lesson.9: A **tuple** is an array with a fixed length where every position has its own type. `[string, number]` is a pair of a string and a number, in exactly this order.
types.lesson.12: The type `any` turns type checking off: you can do anything with the value, even mistakes. The type `unknown` also accepts every value, but you cannot use it until you check what it is. Prefer `unknown` when you do not know a type.
types.card.2: `[string, number]` is a tuple: fixed length, one type per position
types.card.3: `any` turns checking off, `unknown` needs a check first
types.card.4: `typeof x` gives the type name, e.g. `"string"`
types-1.explain: TypeScript has one type for all numbers: `number`. It covers whole numbers and decimals.
types-2.prompt: Which type fits the value `["pen", 2]` as a tuple?
types-2.explain: The first element is a string and the second a number, so the tuple type is `[string, number]`.
types-3.statement: The type of `title` is `string`, even without an annotation.
types-3.explain: TypeScript infers the type from the first value. `"Intro"` is a string, so `title` is a `string`.
types-4.prompt: Complete the annotation for a list of prices.
types-4.explain: A list of numbers has the type `number[]`. `[number]` is a tuple with exactly one number.
types-5.prompt: Which line does the type checker reject?
types-5.explain: `names` is a `string[]`, so you can only add strings. Write `names.push("Dan");` instead.
types-6.explain: The array starts with 3 elements and `push` adds one more, so `length` is `4`.
types-7.prompt: Build a line that creates a tuple `pair` with a string and a number.
types-7.explain: The tuple type `[string, number]` comes after the colon, the value after `=`.
types-8.prompt: What does the type checker say about this code?
types-8.explain: You cannot use a value of type `unknown` before you check its type. With `any`, the code would be accepted.
types-9.prompt: Match the type with its meaning.
types-9.pairs.1: a string followed by a number
types-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so that the program prints `[ 1, 2, 3 ]`.
types-10.explain: Create the empty array first, then `push` adds the numbers in order, and the last line prints the result.
types-11.explain: `10 === 10` is `true` and `+` joins the two strings to `"ab"`.
types-12.statement: With `any`, the type checker still finds typos like `x.lenght`.
types-12.explain: `any` turns checking off, so the typo is accepted and the value is `undefined` at runtime.
functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Write functions with typed parameters and return types, optional and default parameters, arrow functions and void.
functions.lesson.0: A **function** is a named block of code that you can run again and again. Each parameter gets a type, and after the parentheses you write the type of the value that the function returns. `return` gives this value back.
functions.lesson.2: The type checker checks every call. An argument of the wrong type, like `add("2", 3)`, is an error. A missing argument, like `add(1)`, is an error too.
functions.lesson.3: A function that returns nothing has the return type `void`.
functions.lesson.6: A `?` after a parameter name makes the parameter **optional**. If you leave it out, its value is `undefined`.
functions.lesson.8: A parameter with `=` has a **default value**. It is used when you leave the argument out.
functions.lesson.11: An **arrow function** is a short way to write a function: `(n: number) => n * 2`. You usually store it in a `const`. With one expression after `=>`, its value is returned. With curly braces, the body can have several lines and needs `return`.
functions.lesson.13: TypeScript can infer the return type, but writing it helps: the type checker then also checks the code inside the function.
functions.card.1: `b?: string` is optional, `b: number = 1` has a default
functions.card.2: `(n: number) => n * 2` is an arrow function
functions-2.explain: A comparison like `age >= 18` gives `true` or `false`, so the return type is `boolean`.
functions-3.prompt: Which line does the type checker reject?
functions-3.explain: `half` returns a `number`, not a `string`. Write `const result: number = half(10);`.
functions-4.explain: `total(4)` uses the default `2` and returns `8`. `total(4, 3)` returns `12`. Together they are `20`.
functions-5.prompt: Which call does the type checker reject?
functions-5.explain: `y` is optional, but `x` is not. Every call needs at least one number.
functions-6.statement: A function with the return type `void` can return a number.
functions-6.explain: `void` means the function returns nothing. Returning a number from it is an error.
functions-7.prompt: Build an arrow function `square` that returns its parameter times itself.
functions-7.explain: An arrow function is stored in a `const`. After `=>` comes the value it returns.
functions-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so that the program prints `30`.
functions-8.explain: Inside the function, `2 + 1` gives `3` and `3 * 10` gives `30`. You can call `calc` only after it is defined.
functions-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
functions-9.pairs.3: starts the body of an arrow function
functions-9.pairs.4: gives a value back to the caller

functions-11.explain: `n * 3` is a number, so TypeScript infers the return type `number` for `triple`.
functions-12.prompt: Complete the code so that the program prints `Hello, Ben!`.
functions-12.explain: `= "!"` gives `mark` a default value, which is used when the argument is left out.
objects.title: Objects and interfaces
objects.summary: Describe the shape of objects with object types, interfaces and type aliases, including optional and readonly properties.
objects.lesson.0: An **object** groups values under names. These named values are called **properties**. You write an object in curly braces and read a property with a dot.
objects.lesson.2: TypeScript infers the type `{ name: string; age: number }` for this object. You can also write an object type yourself as an annotation. Then you can change the properties, but only with values of the right type.
objects.lesson.5: An `interface` gives an object type a name, so you can use it again and again. An object of this type must have all its properties. A missing property or a misspelled one is an error.
objects.lesson.7: A **type alias** gives a name to any type with the keyword `type`. It works for object types and also for simple types like `string`. For objects, `interface` and `type` work almost the same.
objects.lesson.10: A `?` after a property name makes the property optional: the object may leave it out. A property marked `readonly` gets its value when the object is created and cannot be changed later.
objects.lesson.13: The last line is an error because `id` is `readonly`. Like all types, `readonly` is checked only by the type checker, not while the program runs.
objects.card.3: `readonly id: number` cannot be changed later
objects-1.explain: `truck.wheels` starts at `6` and the second line adds `2`.
objects-2.prompt: Which line does the type checker reject?
objects-2.explain: Every `Pet` needs both properties, but `bird` has no `legs`. Write `{ name: "Kiwi", legs: 2 }`.
objects-3.statement: In an object type, `email?: string` means that the property `email` may be missing.
objects-3.explain: The `?` makes the property optional. If it is missing, reading it gives `undefined`.
objects-4.prompt: Complete the code so that `isbn` cannot be changed after the object is created.
objects-4.explain: In an interface, `readonly` marks a property that cannot be changed. `const` is only for variables.
objects-5.explain: `s.width` is `2` and `s.height` is `5`, so the product is `10`.
objects-6.prompt: Build a type alias `Id` for the type `string`.
objects-6.explain: A type alias starts with `type`, then the name, then `=` and the type.

objects-7.explain: `pears` must be calculated while `apples` is still `3`. Only after that is `apples` set to `0`.

objects-10.explain: `port` is `readonly`, so `c.port = 8080` is rejected. `host` can be changed.
objects-11.statement: The type checker accepts this code.
objects-11.explain: `nme` is not a property of `User`, and `name` is missing. The type checker finds such typos.
unions.title: Union and literal types
unions.summary: Allow several types with |, narrow them with typeof and ===, and limit a value to a few exact choices with literal types.
unions.lesson.0: A **union type** allows more than one type. `number | string` means: a number or a string. The `|` separates the choices.
unions.lesson.2: With a union, you can only use what all its types have in common. `id.toUpperCase()` is an error, because `id` could be a number. You first have to check which type the value has.
unions.lesson.4: An `if` statement runs a block of code only when its condition is `true`. The block after `else` runs when the condition is `false`.
unions.lesson.7: Inside `if (typeof value === "string")`, TypeScript knows that `value` is a string. This is called **narrowing**. In the `else` block, it knows that `value` is a number, so you can use number methods like `toFixed(2)`, which rounds to 2 decimals.
unions.lesson.10: A **literal type** is one exact value, like `"left"`. A union of literal types lists all allowed values. Calling `turn("up")` below would be an error, because `"up"` is not a `Direction`.
unions.lesson.12: Comparing with `===` narrows too. After `if (s === "on")`, TypeScript knows that `s` is `"on"` inside the block, and `"off"` after it, because the function returns inside the block.
unions.card.0: `number | string`: a number or a string
unions-1.explain: `size("hello")` returns the length `5`, and `size(10)` returns `10`. Together they are `15`.
unions-2.prompt: Which line does the type checker reject?
unions-2.explain: `"yellow"` is not one of the allowed values of `Color`. Use `"blue"`, for example.
unions-3.prompt: Complete the check so that the program prints `8`.
unions-3.explain: `typeof` gives the name of the type as a string, so you compare with `"number"` in quotes.
unions-4.statement: The type checker accepts this code.
unions-4.explain: `x` has the type `number | string`, so it can hold a number and later a string.
unions-5.prompt: Which call does the type checker reject?
unions-5.explain: `Size` allows only `"S"`, `"M"` and `"L"`. `"XL"` is not in the list.
unions-7.prompt: Build a type `Answer` that allows only `"yes"` or `"no"`.
unions-7.explain: A union of literal types lists the allowed values, separated by `|`.
unions-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so that the program prints `3`.
unions-8.explain: Inside the `if` block, `x` is a string and has a `length`. Numbers reach `return 0;` after the block.

unions-12.explain: The value could be a number, and numbers have no `toUpperCase()`. Check with `typeof` first.
arrays.title: Working with arrays
arrays.summary: Transform arrays with map, filter, reduce and find, type their callbacks, and copy or combine arrays with spread.
arrays.lesson.0: Arrays have methods that take a function as an argument. This function is called a **callback**: the method calls it for every element. TypeScript knows the element type, so the parameters of the callback get their types automatically.
arrays.lesson.1: `map` creates a **new** array. Each element of the new array is the value that the callback returns. The original array does not change.
arrays.lesson.3: `filter` creates a new array with only the elements for which the callback returns `true`.
arrays.lesson.5: `find` returns the first element for which the callback returns `true`. If there is none, it returns `undefined`, so the type of the result is `string | undefined` here. The string method `startsWith` checks how a string begins.
arrays.lesson.7: `reduce` combines all elements into one value. The callback gets the result so far and the next element. The second argument of `reduce` is the start value.
arrays.lesson.9: You can also write the types of callback parameters and return values yourself. This is common with arrays of objects.
arrays.lesson.11: The **spread** syntax `...` copies all elements of an array into a new array. You can use it to copy or combine arrays.
arrays.lesson.13: Methods that return arrays can be chained: `nums.filter((n) => n > 4).map((n) => n * 10)` first filters, then transforms.
arrays.card.3: `arr.reduce((acc, x) => acc + x, 0)` combines into one value
arrays-1.explain: `map` calls the callback for every element and collects the squares in a new array.
arrays-2.explain: `filter` keeps only the words with more than 3 letters: `"moon"` and `"planet"`.

arrays-3.explain: `reduce` combines all elements into one value, starting with `0`.
arrays-4.explain: `find` returns only the **first** element that matches. `filter` would return `[ 30, 45 ]`.
arrays-5.explain: `map` returns a new array. The original array stays the same.

arrays-6.explain: `find` can return `undefined`, so its result is `string | undefined`. Write `const first: string | undefined = ...`.
arrays-7.prompt: Build a line that keeps only the numbers of `nums` that are greater than 10.

classes.title: Classes
classes.summary: Build classes with fields, a constructor and methods, control access with public, private and readonly, and implement interfaces.
classes.lesson.0: A **class** is a plan for creating objects. It lists **fields** with their types and **methods**, which are functions that belong to the object. The `constructor` runs when you create an object with `new`. Inside the class, `this` means the current object.
classes.lesson.2: Every field must get a value: either directly where you declare it, like `score: number = 0;`, or in the constructor. A field without a value is an error.
classes.lesson.5: Fields and methods are `public` by default: you can use them everywhere. A `private` member can only be used inside its class. A `readonly` field can only be set where it is declared or in the constructor.
classes.lesson.7: Outside the class, `acc.balance` and `acc.owner = "Eve"` are errors. But `private` and `readonly` are checked only by the type checker: when the program runs, they are normal properties, and `console.log` shows them.
classes.lesson.9: An interface can also list methods, like `area(): number;`. With `implements`, a class promises to have everything the interface requires. If a field or method is missing, the type checker reports an error.
classes.lesson.11: A class is also a type. You can write `const p: Player = new Player("Ana");` or use `Player` as a parameter type.
classes.card.2: `private`: only inside the class, `readonly`: set once
classes.card.3: `class Square implements Shape` has all members of `Shape`
classes-1.explain: `items` starts at `0`. The two calls add `3` and `4`.
classes-2.prompt: Which line does the type checker reject?
classes-2.explain: `code` is `private`, so you cannot read it outside the class. Use the public method, for example `s.check(1234)`.

classes-3.explain: Inside a class, `this` is the current object. `this.name = name` stores the parameter in the field.

classes-5.statement: The constructor may set the `readonly` field `x`.
classes-5.explain: A `readonly` field can be set where it is declared or in the constructor, but not later.

generics.title: Generics
generics.summary: Write reusable code with generic functions and interfaces, and use built-in generic types like Partial, Readonly and Record.
generics.lesson.0: Sometimes a function should work with many types and still remember which one it got. `any` would lose this information. **Generics** solve this: a **type parameter** like `<T>` is a placeholder for a type that is filled in at each call.
generics.lesson.2: TypeScript usually infers the type parameters from the arguments. Above, `T` is `number` in the first call and `string` in the second. You can also write them yourself after the function name. A function can have more than one type parameter.
generics.lesson.5: Interfaces and type aliases can have type parameters too. `Box<number>` is a box with a number inside, and `Box<string>` is a box with a string.
generics.lesson.7: You already know a generic type: arrays. `Array<number>` is another way to write `number[]`. Both mean exactly the same type.
generics.lesson.10: TypeScript has useful generic types built in. `Partial<T>` makes all properties of `T` optional. `Readonly<T>` makes all of them `readonly`. `Record<K, V>` is an object with keys of type `K` and values of type `V`.
generics.lesson.12: `fixed.age = 40;` would be an error here, because `fixed` has the type `Readonly<User>`.
generics.lesson.13: Use generics when the type of the output depends on the type of the input. Type parameters often have short names like `T`, `K` and `V`.
generics.card.0: `function first<T>(items: T[]): T` is a generic function
generics.card.1: `interface Box<T> { value: T }` is a generic interface
generics-1.explain: The last position is `length - 1`, which is `2` here, so `last` returns `"z"`.
generics-2.prompt: Complete the code to make `wrap` a generic function.
generics-2.explain: Type parameters go in angle brackets right after the function name: `wrap<T>`.
generics-3.prompt: What type does TypeScript infer for `result`?
generics-3.explain: `T` is filled in from the argument. `word` is a `string`, so `identity` returns a `string`.
generics-4.explain: `Array<string>` is the generic way to write `string[]`. You can use either one.
generics-5.prompt: Which line does the type checker reject?
